slots.writingObjective: Name the change in plain words, as a grounded fact about ShortsOS: an approved short is no longer shown as ready to publish.
One sentence a search result can show: three September 2026 fixes made the review and publishing screens say where a short really stands.

Open with the buyer's stake: a status label is a promise about where a piece of content stands, and a reviewer should grasp it at a glance. Then say ShortsOS found its screens blurring approved, ready and scheduled.
slots.buyerIntent: Can I trust what a status label tells me?

slots.heading: Does approved mean published?
slots.writingObjective: Answer directly: no. Approval is one step, preparing the final file is the next, and publishing is separate again; say what the screens now show at each step.
slots.buyerIntent: Where does my short stand once it is approved?

slots.heading: Three labels that said too much
slots.writingObjective: Describe what the screens said before the fix: an approved item headed as ready, a leftover file shown as final, and a queue titled as scheduled when nothing was scheduled. Then say a real publication's own status still takes precedence over the new badge.

slots.heading: An old decision shown as the current one
slots.writingObjective: Explain the review-card fix: after a short was regenerated, the last decision from an earlier round appeared as if it applied now; it is now labelled as a previous review. Add that the preview could not be watched with sound before deciding, and was fixed the same day.
slots.buyerIntent: Does the reviewer see what they are actually deciding on?

slots.heading: Buttons offered where no decision was possible
slots.writingObjective: Describe the crash: decision buttons were shown on shorts that could not legally be approved, and clicking one failed; decisions are now offered only on a short waiting for review. Close on what a buyer can ask any vendor about its status labels.
slots.buyerIntent: Can the screen offer a decision the system will refuse?
